checked: Every line here is checked by the tests named under it, on every change to AI Juggler. A line without a test can't be added.

groups.title: What it reads, on your Mac only

claims.text: It never reads the passwords, tokens or API keys your tools keep, or the tools' Keychain items. It reads only whether you're signed in, and as which account: its email and organisation.
From Claude Code's settings.json it reads only the settings it needs, each one named in its code and checked.
With crash reports on, it looks through macOS's new crash reports for AI Juggler's own, and keeps only what failed and where.

If you use Claude Squad or Vibe Kanban, it reads their own lists for which repository each of their worktrees belongs to and which config folders their profiles use, and nothing else they keep. It never opens their sign-in or key files.

To show what's open, it reads each tool's own session files: Claude Code's list of running sessions, and from the Claude app only each session's ids, folder, title, times, archived mark and status word, never its summaries. For the Codex app it reads which of its files the app has open. It never reads a running program's environment, where the Claude app keeps a sign-in token.
To know which app and profile a session runs in, it reads the names of running programs, the apps that started them and the options they started with, on your Mac only, and never their environment.
A session's last messages are read from the end of its transcript on your Mac when you open its page, and kept nowhere. One switch in Settings › Desktop apps turns them off.
tests: ui/src/screens/settings/desktop-apps.test.tsx::Last messages are on until you turn them off, and only off is kept
ui/src/pages/session/last-messages.test.tsx::are read only once the page is shown, and once
ui/src/pages/session/last-messages.test.tsx::a paired Mac's session is never read here

claims.text: For a session it runs without a terminal, what the page shows comes from the tool as it works. AI Juggler holds only the latest part, in memory, and never writes it down; the tool keeps its own transcript as it always does.

For sessions other apps run, it keeps each of their processes' program name, start time, the session it was in and a hash of its command line, on your Mac only, for 7 days, so a process left behind can be named by its session. Never its environment, and never the command line itself.
What it keeps lives in its own folder, ~/Library/Application Support/AI Juggler (AI Juggler Nightly for Nightly), and in its own Keychain items.
With Search the words of every session on, its index holds the words to search, not the conversations, in its own folder; turning it off deletes the index.
It never writes to a setup you use where it is, unless you turn on a change that says so first.
It changes your setups and projects only when you apply a change, shows it first, and can undo it.
Copying settings or MCP servers never takes a secret along: the copy names it, and you provide it.

The key you paste for an account added through another service, such as OpenCode Go or Kimi, is kept in AI Juggler's own Keychain item. Only that account's sessions get it, when they start, in the setting their tool reads. It's never written to a file, a log, the search index or a backup, never shown again, and removing the account removes it.
Before you uninstall, it can take out the one setting it may have added to a Claude account, and keep any edits you made since.

Once you say yes, sessions it starts get its agent tools, added to that launch only and never written into your setup: who they are, who's in their pool, what each says it's doing, their own status line, and messages and shared documents with their pool. You can switch them off for a project or a profile.

What an agent sees is up to its pool's level: at Read, who's in the pool, their cards, its own messages and the pool's shared documents; at Work together and Full, also its own status line, sending messages and sharing documents. It sees each account by the name you gave it, never an email or a plan, and only through a connection no one but you on this Mac can open.

Agents in a pool can write to each other and to you. A message waits in its recipient's inbox; it goes into a session as its next prompt only when you click Deliver, or the pool is at Full or you made a rule, and then only between turns, never at a tool's own question or while you type. A session in a terminal is never typed into. Every message says who sent it and that it can't approve anything or change settings.

Messages and shared documents stay in AI Juggler's own data on this Mac, with secrets handled as you chose for packs: anything but Keep replaces them with •••. Loops are capped: a thread pauses after 6 agent messages in a row without you, and two agents answering each other pause the pool until you resume it. Nothing about messages goes over Fleet.

Sessions it starts run your own installed tool, unmodified: Codex through its own app-server, and Claude Code in its terminal, with Claude Code's own hooks added to that launch only so it can say what the session is doing. Nothing is written into your setup. Running Claude Code without a terminal is a Beta you pick for one session at a time.

It stops a process another app's session left running only when you ask, only after that session has ended, and only once it has checked it is the same process it saw. Never the app or the session itself, and no automatic rule ever does it. Each stop is in Cleanup history.
It makes no requests to Anthropic, OpenAI or any other AI provider. Your tools talk to their providers themselves.

It never sits between your tools and their providers: it sets no proxy for them. It sets a provider address only for an account you add through another service, and only the address that service publishes.
It checks GitHub for updates when it starts, if that's on, or when you choose Check now.
Once a day, if that's on, it asks npm's public registry for the newest version of each tool you have an account on, and shows it on that tool's page. It never updates a tool for you.
Usage statistics are off until you choose. When on, they go to stats.figurehead.ai as counts only: never your words, files, paths or names.
Crash reports are kept on your Mac, with names and paths taken out. This version has nowhere to send them.
The Figurehead account is optional. Signed out, nothing goes to it; signed in, a feature you've turned off sends nothing.

Fleet connects only Macs you paired, directly and encrypted, each checking the other's key, and no server carries the traffic. To be found, a Mac announces itself on your local network, and in your Figurehead account if you turn that on.

A paired Mac sees which sessions run where, with their project and account names, states and usage totals. It never gets your sign-ins, files or prompts, and gets a conversation only when you switch one to that Mac.
It never signs in for you. A sign-in is always the tool's own, and AI Juggler never reads the secret the tool saves.
Going to a session never asks for a permission. It uses Accessibility and Automation only when you turned them on in Settings.
It never answers a tool's question or permission prompt by itself. It shows the tool's own choices, sends the one you click to the tool, and records it in the account's log.
It never starts a tool with its permission prompts turned off, and tells Codex it's AI Juggler, never another app.

It never answers a tool's "Trust this folder?" for you, and never lets the tool save the answer to its own config: it asks you once per folder, keeps your answer, and passes it to each session in memory.
tests: ui/src/components/folder-trust.test.tsx::Open restricted keeps that; Cancel stops the launch and keeps nothing

claims.text: It never moves your work to another account by itself. Every switch starts from a click, on this Mac or on a Mac you paired.
tests: ui/src/screens/privacy-page.test.tsx::only the switch screens start a switch

claims.text: Pools only group your sessions. Putting a session in a pool, giving it a role or deleting the pool never starts, stops or types into it.
The test bridge the developers use is not in the app you download.
